speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to raise a matter of extreme importance to shipping industry employees and which has ramifications affecting other industries and other employees. It is regrettable that neither the Minister of Labour nor his parliamentary secretary are here this evening to comment on this vitally important subject.
When the Canada Labour (Standards) Code came into effect it imposed upon industries under federal jurisdiction certain hours of work. One part of the act made it possible for the imposition of these limited hours of work to be deferred for a period of 18 months to permit a formula to be worked out. That was the spirit and intention of the law. Section 53 of the act is worded in such a way that if any person makes application for deferment of the law the imposition of limited hours of work becomes almost indefinitely deferred until the minister makes an order putting into effect certain hours of work or rejects the application to defer that section.
In August of this year meetings were held with employers in the shipping industry. They were held on August 17, and on August 19 meetings were held with union representatives. It is interesting to note that the meetings held on August 19 with union representatives present were held under the auspices of George Haythorne, deputy minister of labour. These meetings were of such a nature that a
December 1, 1966	COMMONS
representative of the employers was in attendance listening to the proposals the unions made in respect of hours of work. But no mention was made of the fact that the employers had made their presentation two days before, and no opportunity was given to the unions to hear what the employers had suggested in order to deal with the hours of work problem. That smacks to me of a little bit of favouritism on one side.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The unions wrote to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) about this matter on September 29 this year. The minister replied on October 13. I will not read his letter in its entirety but will merely make reference to the fact that the minister suggested that the employees and the employers get together and work out some mutually acceptable formula for the application of the hours of work section in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. The minister said that, if necessary, his department stood ready to assist in any way to bring about such meetings. In fact, one of the paragraphs of the minister's letter says that further meetings are planned with both groups in the shipping industry soon in an endeavour to arrive at a satisfactory accommodation on hours of work. I submit that that statement is incorrect. No such meetings were planned and none have been held to date under the auspices of the Department of Labour.
Armed with that letter from the minister saying in effect, sit down and work it out for yourselves, the unions wrote to the Dominion Marine Association, the employers' association, and said, "Let us sit down and work out the hours of work as they apply to the shipping industry." They received a reply on November 23 signed by Philip Hurcomb, general manager of the association, the same individual whom George Haythorne, the deputy minister of labour, permitted to be in attendance at the meeting when the unions made their presentation on August 19. He stated that he had received the letter in which the unions said they would like a meeting in order to arrive at a sensible conclusion on matters set out in the code. He went on to say:
We have today-
November 23, 1966.
-made certain representations to the Minister of Labour as to what steps we consider should be taken . . . Our view in general is that this is a matter for the executive decision of the minister.
In other words, he was saying, it is up to the minister; we are not interested in meeting
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion with you to work out this matter and come to any sensible conclusion. The employers are refusing this meeting because they have made application for deferment. The employees have received almost a life sentence of exemption from the hours of work provisions of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. There is one element in this situation that can bring about some order and that is the government. I submit that it is the direct responsibility of the government, especially when the minister promised in his letter of October 13 that the department and the government would assist in arranging meetings between the parties to see whether they could work out a mutually acceptable formula, to take steps immediately to do so.
It is now 18 months since the act came into effect in July of last year. A principal provision of the act is that no deferment shall take place for a period longer than 18 months. I hope, even though the Minister of Labour has not seen fit to be here this evening and his parliamentary secretary is not here, that somebody on the government side of the house will take this message to the government: For heaven's sake, get off your fanny, get cracking and arrange these meetings in order to bring the full benefits of the law to the employees working in the shipping industry of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I posed a question to the Postmaster General (Mr. C6te) with regard to what I termed rather poor mail service in the province of Nova Scotia. At that time I referred to the fact that the Western Catholic Reporter takes two weeks to reach Nova Scotia from Edmonton, Alberta. This is what has been happening in the past. Also, the Canadian Register has taken seven days to reach Nova Scotia from Kingston, Ontario. This has been brought to my attention by members of the clergy and others concerned.
Someone may say that this is not very important, but I consider it important and I am sure the Postmaster General does also because of the fact that we, as representatives of the people, have a right to bring before this chamber their problems. This is what I am doing at this time. In fact one of the clergy advised me that one issue of a newspaper printed three weeks ago had not arrived yet. He had written the editor of the newspaper in Kingston and in reply was told that it had been mailed very early.
Rather than go into great detail I should like to read an editorial and put it on record. It appeared in the Antigonish Casket, a newspaper published in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, on November 24,	1966. It is entitled
"Threatened Postal Strike" and reads as follows:
Most Canadians must have breathed a sigh of relief last week when the threatened postal strike was averted. We have maintained before, and we repeat our belief, that postal workers have a right to strike even if this should mean considerable disruption in the lives of all Canadians. We do, however, feel that there is something gravely wrong in the Canadian postal service.
Our own experience would indicate that the department spends far too little money to provide a really adequate postal service in the province of Nova Scotia. With practically all of the mail within the province transported by truck rather than by

train, the trucking service is entirely inadequate both as far as accuracy of sorting and frequency of deliveries are concerned.
Before the trucking service was introduced one New York magazine-not a news magazine incidentally-used to reach Antigonish on Monday following its Saturady publication date. Recently, however, we received the November 5 issue of this magazine on November 12, it was followed on November 14 by the issue of October 29 and on November 15 by that of November 12. To take another example, our copy of the National Catholic Reporter of November 2 reached us on November 15; the copy of November 9 arrived on November 16.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Another very notorious example of the complete inadequacy of the present system is the delivery of the Sunday New York Times. This used to arrive in Antigonish on Tuesday almost without fail. Now we hardly ever get it before Wednesday; very often it arrives on Thursday; occasionally it comes on Friday. Surely we have occasion to complain when a newspaper takes from Sunday to Friday to come from New York to Antigonish.
As far as letters mailed within the province are concerned we have equally grave objections. For news stories from the Cape Breton area we rely on telegraph service, but occasionally we need pictures from the Sydney area rather urgently. A picture mailed in the main post office in Sydney on Saturday, however, usually is not delivered in Antigonish until the following Tuesday. A letter mailed Monday morning at the Sydney post office very seldom makes our printing deadline of Tuesday noon.
The root cause of the whole problem is that the Post Office Department will not spend enough money to provide adequate service in Nova Scotia. As in so many other things. Nova Scotians are being shortchanged by their government in Ottawa,
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to pay particular attention to that sentence in the editorial, which I should like to repeat:
As in so many other things, Nova Scotians are being shortchanged by their government in Ottawa.
It is of great importance that Postmaster General Cote and his staff recognize the problem, and to do something about the postal system that is crumbling-at least in Nova Scotia.
I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, knowing the Postmaster General as I do and, as I said this afternoon, having always found him a gentleman in all matters, that he will give this matter his serious consideration and perhaps investigate the problem. I wish to thank him for doing me the courtesy of remaining in the house this evening. I know he is a busy man and could possibly be doing other work but it is an indication of how serious the minister feels the situation is. I hope he will say a few words with reference to this problem so that I can reply to the publishers of this editorial in the Antigonish Casket, as well as to the clergy and other subscribers affected.

Mr. Speaker, first I must say it is always a pleasure lor me to answer a question from the hon. member lor Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir) because to me he represents his constituency and the region from which he comes well. He can be assured that all problems regarding the mails are very important to me. Since he asked me this question I have obtained some information about the Western Catholic Reporter in regard to its mailing and the complaint about the tardiness of its delivery.
First of all, I must say that these publications are all sent second-class mail and they are all moved through the country by the railways or by truck. The normal time for delivery of this publication from Edmonton to Nova Scotia should be approximately four to five days. The reason for this is that it is sent from Edmonton in a mail bag labelled "Province of Quebec and Eastern Provinces". The mail bag takes about three days from Edmonton to Montreal, where the mail is then sorted and sent on to Halifax by train, which takes another 24 hours. It is then sorted again in Halifax and put on trucks for delivery to the different mailing points, which would take another day. If this mail is sent from Edmonton on the Monday there is a possibility that it will arrive in Nova Scotia before the week end. On the other hand, if it is posted on Thursday or Friday it could be delayed because it has to go to Montreal on the week end. The men do not sort mail on Saturday or Sunday, even though there is always a group on duty during the night.
My department received only one complaint relating to the Western Catholic Reporter and this complaint came from Sister Lydia K. Tyszko of Cody International Institute in Antigonish. This complaint was in respect of a
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion non-receipt. I have asked the department to look into the complaint to see why the sister did not receive her publication.
The same problem arises in regard to the Canadian Register. This publication is posted apparently on Thursdays and the mail bag is labelled "Province of Quebec and the Eastern Provinces". It takes about two days to reach Montreal and the mail is then sorted, expedited to Halifax by train and dispatched to the different mailing points by truck. Because of the fact that this publication is mailed on Thursday it can be delayed on Sunday and in addition it might lose another day in Montreal.
There is another reason for mistakes happening in certain types of mail. Because of a relatively small mailing, mistakes can be made when, mistakenly, small mailings are mixed with third-class mail and left aside to be sorted during the week end.
